headline: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: Local AI on your PC is 'quite terrible'
summary: Altman argues that home PCs with RAM are inefficient for AI, preferring cloud-based data centers for better utilization.
details: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has stated that having significant amounts of RAM in personal computers for local AI inference is "quite terrible" from a global resource allocation perspective.

Altman explained that the limited supply of DRAM is better utilized in cloud data centers, where it can achieve maximum utilization, rather than sitting in home computers and being used only a fraction of the time.

This perspective aligns with OpenAI's business model, which primarily relies on closed-source models running in large-scale data centers, rather than enabling widespread local AI execution on consumer hardware.
The sentiment raises concerns among enthusiasts about a future where users might rent AI agents and computing power in the cloud, rather than owning and controlling their own hardware and software.

Altman's comments suggest a belief that data center buildouts will continue and that constant RAM usage in these facilities for AI is more valuable than occasional use for general computing tasks like spreadsheets, web browsing, or gaming.
caption:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman slams local AI on PCs: "It's quite terrible" to have your home computer's RAM used for AI.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has stated that having significant amounts of RAM in personal computers for local AI inference is "quite terrible" from a global resource allocation perspective.

Altman explained that the limited supply of DRAM is better utilized in cloud data centers, where it can achieve maximum utilization, rather than sitting in home computers and being used only a fraction of the time.

This perspective aligns with OpenAI's business model, which primarily relies on closed-source models running in large-scale data centers, rather than enabling widespread local AI execution on consumer hardware.

The sentiment raises concerns among enthusiasts about a future where users might rent AI agents and computing power in the cloud, rather than owning and controlling their own hardware and software.

Altman's comments suggest a belief that data center buildouts will continue and that constant RAM usage in these facilities for AI is more valuable than occasional use for general computing tasks like spreadsheets, web browsing, or gaming.
